div.p: Judge Wakeling Long has passed the ad-vanced Arabic examination, and in the elementary examination the follow have met with success: Mr A. C. McBarnet, Mr. G. H. Hugnes, and Mr. G. H. Fox.

div.head: Mafrouza Tragedy.
div.p: The body of the man who was found murdered near Gabbari on the 27th ult. has at last been identified by the man’s widow as Pandelis Mangos, a Greek who was formerly usher at the Greek Alexandria Consulate. No clue to the murderer has yet found.

div.head: French Pilgrimage
div.p: Some of the members of the French Catholic pilgrimage, led by Monsigno Potard, who have been visiting the Holy Land left Alexandria for France yesterday by the S.S. Congo. The rest of the party will remain in Cairo for a few days more.

div.head: The Fashn Tragedy.
div.p: On Tuesday next the May session of the Greek Assizes will commence. The chief case is that of Cottas who is accused of complicity in the murder of an old Greek woman in Fashn. The actual murderer, a native, was condemned to death and executed a year ago.

div.head: Abduction at Suez.
div.p: A young Greek girl, whose parents live at Port Tewfik, disappeared from her house on Tuesday evening. No traces of her were found until a telegram reached the parents on Thursday informing them that she had run off with a young man, whose suit had not been countenanced by the father and mother. In the telegram the lover demanded permission to marry her, which was immediately granted

div.head: German Gifts to England.
div.p: A German newspaper, in commenting on the resignation of Lord Cromer and his work in Egypt, remarks that England is indebted to Germany for four distinguished men, Lord Cromer, whose family, the Barings, are originally from Bremen, Lord Milner, Lord Geschen, and Sir Ernest Cassel, all of whom have been closely connected with Egypt. The paper goes on to state that all these families became prominent on the day they ceased to be German.

div.head: The Coptic Bazaar Murder.
div.p: As the enquiry is being proceeded with diligently in this case comment is unnecessary while the tragic affair is "sub judice." The nature of the crime, however, is such as to evoke deep sympathy with the Family of the victim, happily this sympathy has taken a very practical form inasmuch as subscription has been started which has already reached upwards of £80, which should be very welcome, as the Lepore family are leaving the country very shortly. Among the leaders of the sub scription is Prince Aziz Hassan, who has dis-! played, a spirit of generosity which has met with universal praise.
